judgment.explanation: The diagnosis correctly identifies DB pool exhaustion in inventory-service as the root cause, with the mechanism attributed to long-lived SELECT pg_sleep(2) sessions occupying all four pool slots. This is materially consistent with the ground truth (four concurrent long queries occupying all four inventory pool slots) — accepting the higher-level accurate mechanism without requiring the exact injection implementation detail. The affected service (inventory-service) is correct. Evidence is independently corroborated: search_logs shows inventory-service PoolTimeout 500 errors with gateway 502 propagation (E-5aea0fbe06a74fc4, E-8574d1ad718f434c), and inspect_database shows four active inventory-service pg_sleep sessions plus 4 ExclusiveLock virtualxid entries (E-89b0d82efabf4864, E-957e201fcb9d475c) — matching both expected evidence points (PoolTimeout and four active inventory SQL sessions). Pool-stats (pool_size 4, pool_max 4) and DB session counts further support saturation. At least two independent supporting observations confirm the mechanism.

regression_risks: Terminating pg_sleep backends is a blunt mitigation; if the issuing workload is legitimate, retries may recreate the sessions and the same pool pressure.
Statement_timeout can cancel long queries that may be needed for correctness or legitimate long-running work, causing incomplete transactions or application errors.
PoolTimeout is itself a symptom-suppression layer: raising pool size or timeouts without locating the pg_sleep issuer could mask the root workload and shift failure to the DB.
No code patch was applied, so the underlying source of SELECT pg_sleep(2) remains able to recur; the incident may regress after the current sessions end.
critic_result.test_sufficiency: Insufficient for full root-cause verification. There is no controlled test, no executed mitigation or fix, and no pool-stats sample showing waiting/available when errors were active. Cross-source symptom evidence is strong (logs, traces, DB active sessions, after-window metrics), but the DB evidence has 34 % omitted sessions/queries and no call deltas, so counterfactual strength is low. A stronger verification would include a pool-stats capture during the incident, a source/workload identification for SELECT pg_sleep(2), an explicit intervention record with before/after pool wait, and confirmation that pool wait time changed.
critic_result.verification_summary: Symptoms are corroborated: inventory-service /products emitted 28 PoolTimeout 500s (E-5aea0fbe06a74fc4), traces show inventory-service GET /products 500 propagating to gateway 502 (E-29e725014eb74ca2), and 3 active inventory-service sessions ran SELECT pg_sleep(2) under PgSleep (E-957e201fcb9d475c). This supports pool starvation as a plausible mechanism for connection-acquisition timeout. However, the causal chain is not fully closed. Only a handful of pg_sleep sessions were observed in a 1.06s DB sample (E-957e201fcb9d475c); 34 % of the DB session/query items were omitted, pg_stat calls_delta was 0 for all fingerprints, and the pool-state evidence is an empty object with unavailable status (E-feb45291decf4898), so max pool size, waiting vs available, and saturation are never directly observed. E-a237cc6f442c46f1 shows the after-window with zero errors, but no fix action or measured intervention is recorded, and the diagnosis is NO_CODE_PATCH, so this cannot establish that terminating pg_sleep or adding statement_timeout caused recovery. The SQL issued by the pg_sleep sessions is not among the pool-timeout request fingerprints in the DB evidence, so the link from pg_sleep to /products DB access is inferential. Verdict: symptom and likely contributor verified; root cause and recovery causal claim only partially verified.

regression_risks: Terminating pg_sleep backends is a blunt mitigation; if the issuing workload is legitimate, retries may recreate the sessions and the same pool pressure.
Statement_timeout can cancel long queries that may be needed for correctness or legitimate long-running work, causing incomplete transactions or application errors.
PoolTimeout is itself a symptom-suppression layer: raising pool size or timeouts without locating the pg_sleep issuer could mask the root workload and shift failure to the DB.
No code patch was applied, so the underlying source of SELECT pg_sleep(2) remains able to recur; the incident may regress after the current sessions end.
critic.test_sufficiency: Insufficient for full root-cause verification. There is no controlled test, no executed mitigation or fix, and no pool-stats sample showing waiting/available when errors were active. Cross-source symptom evidence is strong (logs, traces, DB active sessions, after-window metrics), but the DB evidence has 34 % omitted sessions/queries and no call deltas, so counterfactual strength is low. A stronger verification would include a pool-stats capture during the incident, a source/workload identification for SELECT pg_sleep(2), an explicit intervention record with before/after pool wait, and confirmation that pool wait time changed.
critic.verification_summary: Symptoms are corroborated: inventory-service /products emitted 28 PoolTimeout 500s (E-5aea0fbe06a74fc4), traces show inventory-service GET /products 500 propagating to gateway 502 (E-29e725014eb74ca2), and 3 active inventory-service sessions ran SELECT pg_sleep(2) under PgSleep (E-957e201fcb9d475c). This supports pool starvation as a plausible mechanism for connection-acquisition timeout. However, the causal chain is not fully closed. Only a handful of pg_sleep sessions were observed in a 1.06s DB sample (E-957e201fcb9d475c); 34 % of the DB session/query items were omitted, pg_stat calls_delta was 0 for all fingerprints, and the pool-state evidence is an empty object with unavailable status (E-feb45291decf4898), so max pool size, waiting vs available, and saturation are never directly observed. E-a237cc6f442c46f1 shows the after-window with zero errors, but no fix action or measured intervention is recorded, and the diagnosis is NO_CODE_PATCH, so this cannot establish that terminating pg_sleep or adding statement_timeout caused recovery. The SQL issued by the pg_sleep sessions is not among the pool-timeout request fingerprints in the DB evidence, so the link from pg_sleep to /products DB access is inferential. Verdict: symptom and likely contributor verified; root cause and recovery causal claim only partially verified.
